title: Spring Alignment Check: Why Pothole Season Makes It Essential
body_html:
If you've driven anywhere in Calgary between February and May, your alignment probably isn't where it was last fall. Spring pothole season knocks alignment out faster here than in milder cities, and most drivers don't notice until they see uneven tire wear or feel the steering pull. By then they've burned through a lot of tread that could have lasted another season. Here's why a spring alignment check after pothole season is the highest-return tire-related appointment you can book in Calgary, what to watch for at home, and how to know when it's actually overdue.

Table of Contents

  • Why Spring Is the Critical Alignment Window in Calgary
  • What Actually Knocks Alignment Out
  • 5 Signs Your Alignment Is Off
  • What an Alignment Costs and What's Included
  • Calgary Spring Alignment FAQs

Why Spring Is the Critical Alignment Window in Calgary

Calgary's freeze-thaw cycle wrecks roads. By April every year, our city has thousands of fresh potholes, and any one of them is hard enough to knock toe or camber out of spec on a single hit. Most drivers hit at least one nasty pothole between March and May without thinking much of it — and most cars are running with at least one wheel out of alignment by the time spring tire swaps come around.

The damage compounds. A vehicle 0.5° out of toe alignment can scrub off 30% of the tread on a tire over a single summer of highway driving. A spring alignment catches this before it eats your tires. Our breakdown of spring potholes in Calgary covers what the impacts actually do, and our breakdown of Calgary's worst roads for tires lists the routes where most of this damage starts.

What Actually Knocks Alignment Out

Three things, ranked by frequency in Calgary.

1. Pothole impacts. A wheel slamming into a pothole edge transmits force directly into the suspension. Tie rods, control-arm bushings, and ball joints can shift, all of which change the alignment angles. A single hard hit on Crowchild can put one wheel out of toe by enough to be noticeable.

2. Curb hits. Parallel parking, snow-bank scrapes, and tight-turn impacts all transmit force into the steering knuckle. Curb hits primarily affect camber on the impacted wheel.

3. Worn suspension components. Older vehicles develop play in the tie rods, ball joints, and bushings over time. Once the play is enough to let the alignment angles drift, the alignment "won't hold" — meaning the car needs the underlying parts replaced before another alignment is worth doing.

Calgary's salt and grit accelerate the third problem. Salt corrodes bushing rubber and joint boots faster than dry climates do. Vehicles that live their whole lives here often need bushing replacement at lower mileage than the same vehicle in Vancouver or Victoria.

5 Signs Your Alignment Is Off

  1. The car pulls to one side on a flat, straight road. Find a quiet stretch with no crown, hands lightly on the wheel at 40 km/h. The car should track straight. If it drifts left or right within five seconds, alignment is off.
  2. The steering wheel isn't centred when driving straight. If you're going straight but the wheel sits 5° off to one side, the alignment is out.
  3. Uneven tread wear across one tire. One inner edge worn far more than the outer = camber issue. Both outer edges worn = chronic underinflation. Centre worn = chronic overinflation. Cup-and-scallop pattern = bad shock or out-of-balance wheel.
  4. The vehicle "wanders" at highway speed. Constantly correcting the steering on Deerfoot is a classic sign of toe being off, or worn suspension that won't hold a line.
  5. Vibration paired with a pull. The pothole hit that knocked alignment out often damaged a tire too. Our breakdown on why your steering wheel shakes covers the diagnostic. The pair usually shows up together after a heavy hit, and a road force balance can show whether a wheel took the hit.

If you want to understand the difference between alignment, rotation, and balancing — they're three different services and most people get them confused — see our breakdown.

What an Alignment Costs and What's Included

A standard four-wheel alignment in Calgary runs $90 to $130 for most passenger cars and SUVs. Trucks and vehicles with adjustable rear suspension can go higher. The work includes:

  • Computer measurement of all alignment angles (toe, camber, caster) on all four wheels
  • Adjustment of toe and camber to manufacturer spec where the suspension allows
  • A printed before-and-after report showing what was changed
  • A test drive to confirm the steering wheel is centred and the car tracks straight

If the alignment is well out and the suspension components are worn, the alignment alone may not hold. A reputable shop will tell you that up front and recommend the parts that need replacement first. Bundling alignment with a spring seasonal changeover saves you a second appointment and often catches alignment-related tire wear early enough that the tires can still be saved.

Calgary Spring Alignment FAQs

How often should I get an alignment in Calgary?
Once a year minimum, ideally in spring after pothole season. Drivers who commute Deerfoot or Glenmore daily benefit from a check every six months.

How long does an alignment take?
60 to 90 minutes for a standard four-wheel alignment, plus 30 to 45 minutes if the alignment is bundled with a tire swap.

Can I tell if my alignment is off without a shop visit?
Partly, yes — the five signs above are reliable. But the actual angles need a computer alignment rack to measure precisely.

Will an alignment fix uneven tire wear that's already happened?
No, the worn rubber is gone. An alignment stops further uneven wear from that point forward, but the tire keeps the wear pattern it already has.

Do I need new tires before or after an alignment?
After. New tires installed on an out-of-spec alignment will start wearing unevenly within weeks. Always align before or with new tires, never weeks later.
